To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the “new rural neighborhoods” are a new type of settlement, and that they are the result of the local governments’ efforts in planning and implementing the “New-Typed Urbanization Plan.”

(1) the “Chinese urban dream” has been evolving since the mid-20th century; (2) the “new-typing” of rural urbanization is not a sudden invention of 2014, but has been in the making since the mid- to late 2000s; (3) local variation is enormous; (4) the motivation of local governments to plan for state-led rural development is complex; and (5) local governments are increasingly designing functioning public goods

the new rural neighborhood programs in our case studies were driven by a mix of motives and interests, including the need for local governments to increase their tax base, to reduce the pressure of rural-to-urban migration, and to improve the quality of life of the rural population, and that these programs are often accompanied by the introduction of a new system of land use management that allows for the development of a more comprehensive and balanced system of local planning.

we should be careful when we talk about “urbanization” in China, as there is no one single “new urbanization” policy or plan, but rather a variety of different policies and plans, each with its own specificities.

the “new-typified” urbanization of rural villages in China is a complex, multi-layered and multi-dimensional process, which requires a more detailed analysis at local level to understand how the “new” is actually implemented on the ground, and what it means for local residents and local development.
